title: Data Displays: Comparison, Trend, Uncertainty, Outlier
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Data Displays: Comparison, Trend, Uncertainty, Outlier. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a data display by the question people need to answer: compare categories, follow change over time, locate an outlier, understand a distribution, or inspect uncertainty. Labels, scales, units, baselines, and annotations are part of the representation, not optional decoration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Avoid visual emphasis that implies precision the data does not have. Truncated axes, unexplained aggregation, colour-only categories, and unlabeled targets can change the story people infer. Where uncertainty or missingness matters, make it visible and explain what action remains appropriate.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Start with the judgment, then encode the evidence
turns.text: What changes when we look at start with the judgment, then encode the evidence?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A data display should support a particular comparison or decision: magnitude, ranking, distribution, trend, part-to-whole, relationship, or exception. Choosing a chart by visual novelty invites misinterpretation. Scale, baseline, aggregation, missingness, uncertainty, and annotation determine what the display actually claims.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Uncertainty is explicit. Small samples are not ranked confidently; changing definitions are annotated; unknown accessibility needs are not treated as none; and forecast ranges do not appear as precise promises. Colour is redundant with labels and shape. The team tests whether coordinators can identify a genuine outlier without concluding causation from the display.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: investment performance?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A line rising from a truncated baseline can exaggerate change. Users need period, comparison benchmark, fees, volatility, and uncertainty before treating the trend as evidence for a decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at begin with the decision?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Specify who must compare what, across which period or category, and what action follows. Choose encodings that support that relationship: aligned position and length for comparison, lines for temporal continuity, distributions for variation, and direct annotation for consequential events. Do not choose a chart by fashion.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Provide units, baseline, denominator, time zone, missing data, source, freshness, and filters. Show uncertainty when it affects judgement through ranges, intervals, scenarios, or explicit limitations. Explain outliers without deleting them; they may be errors, rare events, or the most important cases.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use colour redundantly and provide accessible structure, summaries, and data alternatives. Avoid truncated axes, dual scales, area distortions, and aggregation that hides subgroup differences. Test whether people reach the correct decision, not whether they like the graphic.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For dashboards, prioritise status and exception over decorative density. Connect each display to ownership and next action. A visualisation is an interface to evidence, not a neutral picture of reality.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Specify the analytical question and visual claim
turns.text: What changes when we look at specify the analytical question and visual claim?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Scale and aggregation are part of the claim. A truncated axis can exaggerate difference; cumulative totals can hide current deterioration; dual axes invite false relationship; smoothing can erase incidents. Unknown is not zero. Forecasts and estimates use ranges and explanation rather than precise-looking points. Colour is redundant with text and shape.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: investment performance?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A rising line needs period, benchmark, fees, volatility, and uncertainty. A design that makes gain instantly visible while hiding risk supports persuasion, not an informed financial judgment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ask what decision the chart will change. If no decision exists, a visually rich display may be monitoring theatre rather than useful information.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Every data display should support a decision. Identify the comparison, baseline, time window, unit, population, uncertainty, and action before selecting a chart or table. Use direct labels and accessible alternatives where they reduce interpretation work. Treat outliers and missing data as information to investigate, not visual noise to hide.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A display that communicates confidence and limitation can prevent false precision.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Chart-first design: a familiar visual is chosen before the decision or data relationship is clear. False precision: tiny differences are emphasised without uncertainty, scale, or practical meaning. Context loss: date range, denominator, baseline, or segment is absent. Inaccessible encoding: essential meaning depends only on colour, position, or hover interaction.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A dashboard shows a smooth green line rising. The person cannot tell the period, baseline, sample size, target, or whether one sudden jump is an error. The chart looks reassuring while concealing the decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a chart in a product. Write the question it answers, its unit, time range, baseline, and one uncertainty the design hides.
